title: Event Manager Salary: How to Convert Your Hourly Rate to Annual Pay
description: Learn how to calculate your event manager salary from an hourly rate. Includes tax, super, and award rates for event managers in Australia.

bodyMarkdown:
## Converting Your Hourly Rate to Annual Pay

If you’re an event manager comparing job offers or negotiating a salary, understanding how your hourly rate translates to annual pay is essential. The standard formula is straightforward:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

This calculation assumes you work the same number of hours every week, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, allowances, or salary sacrifice. For full-time employees, the typical week is 38 hours (the ordinary hours used by the Fair Work Commission). For example, an event manager earning $35.00 per hour would have an annual salary of:

$35.00 × 38 × 52 = $69,160 before tax and super.

If you are paid fortnightly, your gross pay is simply your weekly pay multiplied by two. Using the same example, weekly pay is $1,330, so fortnightly pay is $2,660.

## Understanding the National Minimum Wage and Award Rates

The National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. This is the legal minimum for award/agreement-free employees. However, most event managers are covered by the Amusement, Events and Recreation Award (MA000080). This award sets higher minimum pay rates based on classification levels (e.g., Level 4 or Level 5 for experienced event managers). You can find the exact rates in the [pay guides](/blog) published by the Fair Work Ombudsman.

To give you context, the Australian Bureau of Statistics’ Average Weekly Earnings (May 2026) shows full-time adult ordinary time earnings of $2,083.70 per week, or about $108,352 annually. All employees (including part-time) average $1,579.20 per week. An event manager salary may fall below or above these averages depending on experience, location, and employer.

### Casual Loading

If you work as a casual event manager, you are entitled to a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate. This compensates for not receiving paid annual leave, personal leave, or other entitlements. For example, if the award rate for your classification is $30.00 per hour, your casual rate becomes $37.50 per hour. The [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) is applied before calculating annual pay.

## Superannuation and Tax

### Super Guarantee

Your employer must pay superannuation guarantee contributions of 12% of your ordinary earnings, on top of your salary. This is not deducted from your pay; it is an additional benefit. The super guarantee is capped at the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year (2026–27). For an event manager earning $69,160 annually, the super contribution would be $8,299.20 per year.

### Tax and Medicare

Income tax for 2026–27 is calculated using the resident tax scale:
- Nil tax on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Most residents also pay a Medicare levy of 2% (with possible reductions for low-income earners). The Medicare levy reduction thresholds used here are based on 2025–26 figures, as the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed. For a single person earning $69,160, the estimated tax (including Medicare) would be approximately $12,000–$13,000, leaving a take-home pay of around $56,000–$57,000 per year.

## Using the Pay Calculator

To get a personalised estimate, you can use the [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) tool on this site. Enter your base hourly rate (before casual loading) and select whether you are casual. The calculator will show your annual, monthly, fortnightly, and weekly gross pay, along with estimated tax and super. Remember, this is an estimate only – your actual pay may vary due to overtime, allowances, salary packaging, or HELP repayments.

For a deeper look at award rates, visit the [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page or browse the [pay guides](/blog) for your specific award.

## Key Differences in Ordinary-Time Earnings

It’s important to distinguish between different earnings measures:
- **National Minimum Wage**: $26.44/hour (award-free employees)
- **Award rates**: Higher, depending on classification (e.g., event manager Level 4 may be $28–$32/hour)
- **ABS Average Weekly Earnings (full-time ordinary time)**: $2,083.70/week – reflects all full-time employees, not just event managers
- **All employees average**: $1,579.20/week – includes part-time workers

Your event manager salary will likely fall somewhere between the award minimum and the national average, depending on your experience and employer.

## Final Thoughts

Converting your hourly rate to annual pay is a useful first step in understanding your compensation. But remember to factor in superannuation (paid on top), casual loading (if applicable), and tax. Always check the relevant award or enterprise agreement for your exact entitlements. The Fair Work Ombudsman provides free resources, including pay guides and a pay calculator, to help you get accurate figures.
